articles.author: Mohith
articles.description:
My Thinking and Approach



  
  
  Introduction


In this problem, I was given a sorted linked list and asked to remove duplicate elements.
Since the list is already sorted, duplicates will always appear next to each other. This made the problem easier to approach.
Given a sorted linked list
Remove duplicate nodes
Return the updated list
Initially, I thought:
Store elements in a set
Rebuild the linked list
But this uses extra space, which is not required here.
Because the list is sorted:
Duplicate values are always adjacent
So I only need to compare current node with the next node
I decided to:
Traverse the list once
If current node value equals next node value:
Skip the next node
Otherwise:
Move forward
Start with curr = head

Traverse while curr and curr.next are not null
If curr.data == curr.next.data:
Remove duplicate by skipping node
curr.next = curr.next.next
Else:
Move to next node
class Solution {
    Node removeDuplicates(Node head) {
        Node curr = head;

        while (curr != null && curr.next != null) {
            if (curr.data == curr.next.data) {
                curr.next = curr.next.next;
            } else {
                curr = curr.next;
            }
        }

        return head;
    }
}

Input:
2 → 2 → 4 → 5
Compare 2 and 2 → remove duplicate
List becomes → 2 → 4 → 5



Output:
2 → 4 → 5
Time Complexity: O(n)
Space Complexity: O(1)
Sorted property simplifies the problem
No need for extra space
Pointer manipulation is important in linked lists
This problem helped me understand how to efficiently handle duplicates in linked lists. It also reinforced the importance of using problem constraints (like sorted order) to simplify the solution.
articles.title: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Linked List –CA23

articles.author: Mohith
articles.description:
My Thinking and Approach



  
  
  Introduction


In this problem, I was given the head of a singly linked list and asked to reverse it.
At first, I thought it might be tricky because linked lists don’t allow direct indexing like arrays. But once I understood how pointers work, the solution became clear.
Given the head of a singly linked list
Reverse the list
Return the new head
Initially, I thought:
Store elements in an array
Reverse the array
Rebuild the linked list
But this uses extra space and is not efficient.
So I tried to solve it directly using pointers.
I realized that:
Each node points to the next node
To reverse, I need to change the direction of these pointers
Use three pointers:
prev → previous node
curr → current node
next → next node
Initialize:
prev = null
curr = head
Traverse the list:
Store next node → next = curr.next

Reverse pointer → curr.next = prev

Move prev forward
Move curr forward
At the end:
prev becomes the new head
class Solution {
    Node reverseList(Node head) {
        Node prev = null;
        Node curr = head;

        while (curr != null) {
            Node next = curr.next;
            curr.next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = next;
        }

        return prev;
    }
}

Input:
1 → 2 → 3 → 4
Reverse 1 → null
Reverse 2 → 1
Reverse 3 → 2
Reverse 4 → 3
Output:
4 → 3 → 2 → 1
Input:
2 → 7 → 10 → 9 → 8
Output:
8 → 9 → 10 → 7 → 2
Time Complexity: O(n)
Space Complexity: O(1)
Linked lists require pointer manipulation
Always store next node before changing links
Iterative approach is simple and efficient
This problem helped me understand how linked lists work internally. It improved my confidence in handling pointer-based problems and showed how simple logic can reverse an entire data structure efficiently.
articles.title: Reverse a Linked List – CA22
